Stage 4 · Grammar

Must, have to, can’t, should, needn’t

Five small words that decide whether you are allowed to keep the gold.

MeaningFormExample

4 · One situation, five instructions.
You must report it.  →  I am the one telling you.
You have to report it.  →  the law says so, not me.
You mustn’t report it.  →  reporting it is forbidden.
You don’t have to report it.  →  report it or not, as you like.
You should report it.  →  it would be wise to.
1 · Read the explanation.
Where the obligation comes from

English has two ways of saying that something is necessary, and they are not interchangeable. Must carries the speaker’s own authority: the person speaking is the source of the obligation. Have to reports an obligation that exists outside the conversation — a law, a company rule, a timetable, a doctor. In the news items you heard, everything is have to, because the reporter is describing the law rather than giving anybody orders.

In practice, spoken British English uses have to far more often than must, and must survives mainly in written rules and in strong personal recommendations: You must see that film.

The negatives are the difficult part
  • mustn’t = it is forbidden. You mustn’t sell it.
  • don’t have to / needn’t = it is not necessary. You don’t have to sell it.
  • These two are opposites, not variations. Mustn’t closes the door; don’t have to opens it.
  • can’t covers prohibition too, and often sounds more natural than mustn’t in speech: You can’t park there.
2 · Study the examples.
MeaningExample
law or ruleFinders have to report valuable objects to the police.
law or rule, pastThe couple had to hand the coins over to an official.
law or rule, futureThey will have to wait for the court’s decision.
speaker’s own authorityYou must tell me exactly where you found it.
written regulationAll valuables must be handed in at the desk.
prohibitionYou mustn’t sell it while the claim is being heard.
prohibition, spokenYou can’t keep money that you know is somebody else’s.
no obligationHe doesn’t have to pay anything to make a claim.
no obligation, formalYou needn’t bring the receipt.
no obligation, pastThey didn’t have to give the diamonds back.

Two things to watch

1 — Must has no past. The past of must (obligation) is had to, never musted: They had to hand the coins over. The form must have exists, but it means something completely different — a guess about the past, which is lesson 6.

2 — Needn’t is not the negative of must. The negative of must as an obligation is needn’t or don’t have to. Mustn’t is a different instruction altogether: it forbids.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Where the obligation comes from

Must and have to both impose an obligation, but they point at different sources. Must comes from the speaker: it is the form of notices, rules you are issuing and things you have decided yourself — You must tell me where you found it, I must stop putting this off. Have to reports an obligation that comes from outside — a law, a policy, a timetable: They have to hand the coins to an official. In speech, have to is far commoner; a native speaker who says I must is usually talking about their own resolve.

Must has no infinitive, no past and no future, so have to supplies the missing forms: I had to hand it in, You will have to sign it, He hates having to ask. It also has no do-support: Must I sign? but Do I have to sign?

The pair that traps everybody: mustn't and don't have to

These are not two ways of saying the same thing. You mustn’t sell it forbids the action. You don’t have to sell it removes the obligation and leaves you free to choose. The negative of have to is not a prohibition at all; the prohibition is mustn’t or, more conversationally, can’t: You can’t take photographs in here.

Needn’t behaves like don’t have to and sounds slightly more British and slightly more formal. For permission, can is the everyday form and may the formal one; for advice, should and ought to are interchangeable, with ought to a little more emphatic about what is right rather than what is sensible.

Errors to watch: I must to go → I must go · He musts sign it → He must sign it · Yesterday I must wait an hour → I had to wait · You mustn’t come if you are busy (that forbids it) → You don’t have to come.

Lost property: what the law says
Anything you find in a public place be handed to the police within two weeks. You sell or give away an item while the case is open, even if you are sure nobody wants it. You pay anything to make a claim, and you attend in person if you send the form by post. Owners prove ownership before an item is released. If nobody claims the item within a year, the finder keep it, although the police always advise that you keep the receipt.

1 · Read the model comment.
Model · a comment on file 1

Everybody in this thread keeps saying the cleaner has to hand the money in. She does — but that is the least interesting part of it.

The legal position is simple enough. The guest’s address is on the booking, so the owner can be found, and in most countries that means she mustn’t keep the cash: it is not lost property in the useful sense, it is somebody’s money that they left behind. She doesn’t have to run round the city looking for him; she needn’t even ring him. She only has to give it to the hotel and get a receipt.

What she should do is a separate question. Hotels are not famous for passing on cash, and if I were her I would ask for the handover in writing. And if the guest never claims it, she can reasonably expect a share — the man who found $200,000 of diamonds in the street got a reward, and he had far less trouble than she will.
